title: Who Was REALLY Buying Stocks Yesterday?
summary: Wall Street celebrated its best day in nineteen months. Was it genuine investor conviction or simply hedge funds scrambling to cover short positions?
body_markdown:
*Wall Street celebrated its best day in nineteen months. Was it genuine investor conviction or simply hedge funds scrambling to cover short positions?*


***KEY TAKEWAYS***


-


Stocks staged a historic rebound. The S&P 500 gained 4.73%, the Nasdaq Composite surged 6.51%, and the Dow added 1,448 points, with 417 S&P 500 constituents finishing higher.


-


Short covering fueled the rally. Hedge funds entered Monday following aggressive short selling, while Goldman Sachs estimated that trend-following funds had sold approximately $57 billion in stocks over the preceding month.


-


Monetary conditions remained unchanged. The 10-year Treasury yield held near 4.92%, while futures markets continued to assign a greater than 90% probability to a December Fed rate hike.


-


Valuations expanded without corresponding earnings revisions. The S&P 500’s forward P/E multiple climbed from approximately 17 to 18, while Nvidia analysts raised price targets without corresponding increases in earnings estimates, according to the accounts cited.


-


AI profitability remains under scrutiny. Hewlett Packard Enterprise reported 50% revenue growth and raised its outlook, but its shares fell in extended trading after management indicated that AI profit margins would deteriorate next year.


***MY HOT TAKES***


-


Forced buying should not be confused with investor conviction. Short sellers purchasing shares to close positions create demand, but that demand disappears once their positions are closed.


-


The bond market’s indifference deserves more attention than the stock market’s enthusiasm. Yesterday’s rally did nothing to improve the interest rate environment in which companies must finance operations and investors must value future earnings.


-


Multiple expansion is a less dependable foundation for a recovery than earnings growth. Investors became willing to pay more for essentially the same expected earnings, leaving the rally vulnerable to another shift in sentiment.


-


The AI trade is increasingly becoming a profitability trade. HPE’s post-earnings decline suggests that investors are no longer willing to reward spectacular revenue growth without examining what ultimately reaches the bottom line.


-


Yesterday was encouraging, but it was not conclusive. Broad participation satisfies one important condition for a sustainable bottom, but earnings durability and the extent of remaining market leverage still need to be established.


-


You can quote me: *“A multiple can change its mind in an afternoon–we just watched it happen twice in two sessions. Earnings take quarters.”*


***Is it in line or on line?*** The longest line in the store is not at the register. Go to any department store the morning after Christmas and you will see it–forty people deep, snaking past the perfume counter, everybody holding a bag. Busy place! Booming, you would think. Except nobody in that line is buying anything. They are giving something BACK. The sweater that didn’t fit. The air fryer nobody asked for. 🤣 I have stood in that line more than once, usually holding something my wife picked out for somebody else. Here is the thing. From the parking lot, a store full of returns and a store full of shoppers look EXACTLY the same. Full lot. Long lines. Lots of commotion. Yesterday the S&P 500 jumped…no, leapt 4.7%–its best day since last April–and Wall Street looked like the busiest store in America. So I did what I always do. I walked inside to see which line everybody was standing in. Hold that thought.


Let me start with who was standing in it. Hedge funds spent last week doing something they had not done with this much enthusiasm since June of 2022–selling stocks short (borrowing shares, selling them, and hoping to buy them back cheaper later). Goldman Sachs’ prime brokerage desk, which sees what the big funds are actually doing, counted 1.4 shares sold short for every share bought outright. The computer-driven funds that follow trends were right there with them. By Goldman’s estimate they sold about $57 billion of stock in a month and wound up betting against the market to the tune of roughly $19 billion. That is a LOT of borrowed merchandise walking around.


Then came Monday. Around nine in the morning–before the ink even dried on my blogpost–Nvidia’s board put Jensen Huang back in the CEO chair, eleven days after he resigned. The stock finished the day up more than 31%. Now, if you had borrowed those shares and sold them, that announcement was not good news. That was the store manager getting on the loudspeaker to say the returns desk closes in ten minutes.


Everybody ran for the same counter. Goldman keeps a basket of the most heavily shorted stocks, and that basket jumped 5.73% on the day. Its trading desk, by one account I read this morning, rated the day’s activity a five out of ten–funds were busy closing out bets AGAINST stocks, not placing new bets on them. The long-term money that had been selling Nvidia for two weeks mostly stayed on the sidelines. 🧐– a five out of ten. On the best day in nineteen months. Does that sound like a stampede of eager shoppers to you?


From the parking lot, of course, it looked spectacular. The S&P 500 gained 4.73%. The Nasdaq Composite jumped 6.51%. The Dow added 1,448 points. And I will give credit where it is due–this was not five stocks dragging an index uphill. Some 417 of the 500 companies in the S&P finished higher. Technology gained almost 9%. The only two sectors that fell were energy and consumer staples–the toothpaste-and-canned-soup stocks people had been hiding in the week before. Wall Street’s fear gauge, the VIX, dropped about 26%.


Impressive. Now the cold water–sorry. Monday won back about half of what the index lost last week. HALF. By my math, the S&P is still better than 7% below the record it set on October 6. A terrific day inside a rough month is still…well, a rough month.


What interests me more than what moved is what DIDN’T. The yield on the 10-year Treasury finished the day at roughly 4.92%–right where it started. On the best day for stocks since the spring of last year, the bond market did not so much as look up from its newspaper. The Fed did not blink either. Futures traders still put the odds of a rate HIKE on December 9 north of nine in ten, and the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge arrives tomorrow morning at 8:30, with economists expecting the core rate to tick UP to 3.2% from 3.1%. And earnings? Wall Street’s analysts fell over themselves raising their price targets on Nvidia overnight. By the accounts I have seen, nobody raised an EARNINGS estimate. Same companies. Same forecasts. Same interest rates. Different price.


Here is why that matters to you as an investor. A stock price is two numbers multiplied together–what a company earns, and what investors are willing to pay for each dollar of those earnings (the P/E ratio, or the multiple, if you want to sound like you work on Wall Street). Before Monday, the S&P 500 was trading at about 17 times expected earnings, well under its five-year average of nearly 20. Tack on Monday’s gain and you are somewhere near 18. Still not expensive by recent standards. But notice which of the two numbers did the work. The multiple went up. The earnings stayed home. A multiple can change its mind in an afternoon–we just watched it happen twice in two sessions. Earnings take quarters.


We did get a look at some actual earnings last night. Hewlett Packard Enterprise–a big seller of the servers that fill AI data centers–reported revenue up 50% from a year ago, beat estimates, and raised its forecast for next year. The stock had already run up better than 17% during the day. After the report? It FELL nearly 7%, and it’s down by some 12% in this morning's pre-market. Why? Because management said profit margins in its AI business would be thinner next year–about 14%, down from better than 18% last quarter. Sales up by half, guidance raised, and the stock goes down on margins. That is a market that has stopped paying for revenue and started asking what is left after the bills are paid. Dell reports tonight after the close. It will get the same question.


Yesterday, before all of this Nvidia drama hit the tape, I told you that a bounce and a bottom look identical on day one, and that three things would eventually tell them apart–how many stocks join in, whether earnings hold up, and whether the borrowed money has left the building. One day later, here is my tally. Participation showed up. Earnings showed up with an asterisk. And the borrowed money–I still can’t tell you, because the next official count of margin debt has not been published. A pass, a maybe, and an incomplete. I have seen worse report cards. I have brought home worse report cards. 🤣


A word about big days, because I have lived through a few of them. They are not what they appear. Wells Fargo once went back through thirty years of trading and found that ALL TEN of the best days for the S&P 500 landed in the middle of either the financial crisis or the pandemic crash. 👀 In October of 2008, the index had two separate days of better than 10%. The bottom was still five months and a lot of heartache away. Calm, healthy markets rarely do that sort of thing. Stressed ones do it regularly.


But–and this is an important but–sometimes the big day IS the turn. The last time the S&P had a better day than Monday’s was April 9, 2025, when it soared 9.5%. The low for that entire year had been set at the close the day before. So no, a big day is not a warning. It is not an all-clear either. It is a thermometer. It tells you the patient is running a fever. It does not tell you which way the fever is headed.


I am not here to rain on a 1,448-point parade. Forced buying is still buying, and a market that was priced for disaster on Friday is priced for something less than disaster this morning. That counts. Stocks are cheaper than they were in early October, the companies behind them are still making money, and Monday proved that the bears can be wrong in a hurry, too.


But a returns line has one defining feature. It ENDS. Once the last borrowed share is handed back across the counter, that customer is finished–he is not coming back tomorrow for more. As I write this, Nvidia is giving back about 5% before the opening bell, and stock futures are bouncing around, mostly in the red. The returns desk, it seems, is quiet this morning. What happens next depends on the other line. The slow one. The one at the register, where people reach for their own wallets because they looked at the merchandise, looked at the price tag, and decided all on their own that they wanted it.


That line was short on Monday. It may well be longer by the end of the week–Dell’s numbers tonight and the inflation report tomorrow morning will have plenty to say about it. So enjoy the green on your screen. After last week, you have earned it. Then do what I do on the morning after Christmas. Walk right past the crowd at the returns desk, find the register, and count heads. And whatever you picked up on Monday–keep the receipt. 😉


***YESTERDAY’S MARKETS***


*Stocks staged their biggest rally since April 2025 on Monday, with the S&P 500 up 4.73% and the Nasdaq Composite up 6.51%, after Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive. A 1,447-point advance left the Dow Jones Industrial Average at 49,595. Nvidia shares ended the day 31.5% higher, and technology paced a broad advance in which only energy and consumer staples lost ground. Crude finished lower, with West Texas Intermediate down 4.5% at $80.17 a barrel, while the 10-year Treasury yield held at 4.92%.*


***NEXT UP***


-


FHFA House Price Index (September) is looking like an 0.2% gain after it grew by -0.3% in August.


-


Conference Board Consumer Confidence (November) may have risen to 92.4 from 91.7.


-


Important earnings today: ***Dollar Tree, Burlington, Dick’s Sporting Goods, JM Smucker, Kohl’s, Best Buy, Analog Devices, Abercrombie & Fitch, Dell, Workday, Ambarella, Autodesk, Nutanix, Cleanspark,*** and ***HP Inc.***
